topics.title: Voltage, Current, and Resistance: The Big Three

hook.text: Electricity has three fundamental properties. Understand them and every circuit makes sense.

buildup.text: Voltage is electrical pressure — it pushes electrons. Current is how many electrons flow per second. Resistance opposes that flow.

discovery.text: Ohm's Law ties them together: voltage equals current times resistance. Change one and the others shift.

twist.text: A 10,000-volt static shock is harmless because the current is tiny. It's current that kills, not voltage alone.

climax.text: Every circuit from a flashlight to a supercomputer obeys Ohm's Law. It's the foundation of electrical engineering.

punchline.text: Pressure, flow, and friction. Three numbers explain all of electricity.

quiz.question: Why is a 10,000-volt static shock harmless?
options: The voltage drops to zero before reaching your heart
The current is extremely small despite the high voltage
Static electricity travels only on the skin surface

topics.title: AC vs. DC: The War of Currents

hook.text: Edison backed DC. Tesla championed AC. The fight shaped the entire electrical grid we use today.

buildup.text: DC flows in one direction — batteries produce it. AC reverses direction 50 or 60 times per second.

discovery.text: AC wins for transmission because transformers can step voltage up for long distances and down for safe delivery.

twist.text: Edison publicly electrocuted animals with AC to prove it was dangerous. He lost the technical argument anyway.

climax.text: Today, HVDC lines carry power over thousands of kilometers more efficiently than AC. DC is making a comeback.

punchline.text: AC won the war. DC is winning the rematch.

quiz.question: Why did AC win over DC for the original power grid?
options: AC generators were cheaper to manufacture in the 1890s
Transformers can step AC voltage up and down for efficient long-distance transmission
AC is safer for household use than DC at the same voltage

topics.title: Electromagnetic Induction: How We Generate Electricity

hook.text: Move a magnet through a coil of wire and electricity flows. Michael Faraday discovered this in 1831.

buildup.text: A changing magnetic field induces an electromotive force in a conductor. Faster changes mean more voltage.

discovery.text: Every generator on Earth uses this principle. Spinning magnets past coils produce alternating current.

twist.text: The process works in reverse too. Run current through a coil near a magnet and it spins — that's a motor.

climax.text: Coal plants, wind turbines, and hydroelectric dams all spin magnets inside coils. The source changes, the physics doesn't.

punchline.text: Spin a magnet. Get electricity. Faraday changed the world.

quiz.question: What is the relationship between a generator and an electric motor?
options: They use completely different physical principles to operate
They are the same process in reverse: one converts motion to current, the other current to motion
A generator uses magnets but a motor uses electromagnets

topics.title: Conductors and Insulators: Why Copper but Not Rubber

hook.text: Copper carries electricity. Rubber stops it. The difference is whether electrons can move freely.

buildup.text: In conductors, outer electrons aren't tightly bound to atoms. An electric field pushes them along like a river.

discovery.text: Insulators grip their electrons tightly. Even strong voltage can't pry them loose — until it can, and that's a spark.

twist.text: Semiconductors sit between the two. Silicon barely conducts on its own, but add impurities and it becomes controllable.

climax.text: Every computer chip is built from semiconductor junctions. The entire digital age depends on silicon's switchable conductivity.

punchline.text: Free electrons: conductor. Locked electrons: insulator. Switchable: revolution.

quiz.question: What makes semiconductors special compared to conductors and insulators?
options: They conduct only at high temperatures, acting as safety switches
Adding impurities makes their conductivity controllable and switchable
They are lighter than both conductors and insulators

topics.title: Grounding: Earth as an Electrical Safety Net

hook.text: The third prong on your plug connects to a copper rod buried in the ground outside your house.

buildup.text: Earth is a massive conductor. Grounding provides a safe path for fault current — electricity takes it instead of you.

discovery.text: If a wire breaks loose inside an appliance, ground fault current trips the breaker before anyone gets shocked.

twist.text: Lightning rods work the same way. They provide a preferred path to ground so lightning skips the building.

climax.text: GFCIs detect imbalances as small as 5 milliamps and cut power in 25 milliseconds. They save hundreds of lives yearly.

punchline.text: Give electricity an easier path. It won't go through you.

quiz.question: How does a GFCI protect people from electrical shock?
options: It limits voltage to a safe level throughout the entire circuit
It detects tiny current imbalances and cuts power within milliseconds
It insulates the ground wire so no current can flow to earth

topics.title: Superconductors: Zero Resistance, Absolute Cold

hook.text: Cool certain materials below -200 degrees C and their electrical resistance drops to exactly zero.

buildup.text: With zero resistance, current flows forever without losing energy. No heat, no waste, no power loss.

discovery.text: Heike Kamerlingh Onnes discovered superconductivity in mercury in 1911. He cooled it with liquid helium.

twist.text: Superconductors also repel magnetic fields completely. Magnets levitate above them — the Meissner effect.

climax.text: MRI machines use superconducting coils cooled by liquid helium. They generate magnetic fields 60,000 times Earth's.

punchline.text: Cool it enough and resistance vanishes. Physics allows free electricity.

quiz.question: What is the Meissner effect in superconductors?
options: Current increases exponentially as temperature decreases below the threshold
Superconductors completely repel magnetic fields, causing magnets to levitate
Electrical resistance fluctuates rapidly near the critical temperature

topics.title: Resistors: Controlling the Flow

hook.text: Without resistors, every LED would burn out instantly. Resistors limit current to safe levels.

buildup.text: Resistance is measured in ohms. Higher resistance means less current flows for a given voltage.

discovery.text: Colored bands on resistors encode their value. Brown-black-red means 1,000 ohms — a code invented in the 1920s.

twist.text: Resistors convert excess electrical energy into heat. That's useful in toasters but wasteful in circuits.

climax.text: Voltage dividers use two resistors to produce any fraction of the input voltage. Simple parts, precise control.

punchline.text: Too much current? Add a resistor. Problem solved.

quiz.question: What do the colored bands on a resistor indicate?
options: The maximum voltage the resistor can handle safely
The resistance value in ohms encoded in a standard color code
The manufacturer and date of production

topics.title: Capacitors: Tiny Batteries That Charge Instantly

hook.text: A camera flash charges for seconds, then dumps all its energy in a millisecond. That's a capacitor.

buildup.text: Two metal plates separated by an insulator store charge. Voltage builds as electrons pile up on one plate.

discovery.text: Capacitance is measured in farads. Most electronic capacitors are microfarads — millionths of a farad.

twist.text: Supercapacitors bridge the gap between capacitors and batteries. They charge in seconds and last millions of cycles.

climax.text: Every power supply uses capacitors to smooth voltage. Without them, your devices would flicker with every AC cycle.

punchline.text: Store charge fast. Release it faster. That's a capacitor.

quiz.question: What advantage do supercapacitors have over regular batteries?
options: They store far more total energy in the same physical volume
They charge in seconds and survive millions of charge-discharge cycles
They produce higher voltage for more powerful applications

topics.title: Inductors: Magnetism Meets Electricity

hook.text: An inductor resists changes in current. Try to increase the flow and it pushes back magnetically.

buildup.text: A wire coil creates a magnetic field when current flows. Changing the current changes the field, inducing opposing voltage.

discovery.text: Inductance is measured in henrys. It depends on the number of coil turns, core material, and coil dimensions.

twist.text: Transformers are two inductors sharing a magnetic core. Energy transfers between them without any electrical connection.

climax.text: Wireless phone chargers use induction. A coil in the pad creates a field that a coil in the phone captures.

punchline.text: Coil some wire. Run current through it. Magnetism does the rest.

quiz.question: How do wireless phone chargers transfer energy?
options: Microwaves carry energy from the pad to the phone's antenna
A coil in the pad creates a magnetic field that a coil in the phone captures via induction
Tiny electrical contacts in the pad connect to the phone case

topics.title: Transformers: Stepping Voltage Up and Down

hook.text: Power leaves a plant at 400,000 volts and arrives at your outlet at 120 or 240. Transformers make that possible.

buildup.text: A transformer has two coils around an iron core. The turns ratio determines voltage change. More turns means more voltage.

discovery.text: Step-up transformers increase voltage for transmission. Step-down transformers reduce it for homes. Same device, different ratios.

twist.text: Transformers only work with AC. That's why Edison's DC system couldn't compete — no way to change voltage efficiently.

climax.text: Modern transformers exceed 99% efficiency. Almost no energy is lost in the conversion process.

punchline.text: Two coils. One core. Voltage goes up or down on demand.

quiz.question: Why can't transformers work with DC power?
options: DC voltage is too low for the coils to generate a magnetic field
Transformers need a changing magnetic field, which only AC provides
DC current would melt the iron core due to excessive heat

topics.title: Diodes: One-Way Streets for Electricity

hook.text: A diode lets current flow in one direction and blocks it completely in the other. It's an electrical check valve.

buildup.text: A junction between P-type and N-type semiconductor creates a one-way barrier for electrons.

discovery.text: Rectifiers use four diodes to convert AC to DC. Every phone charger has a rectifier bridge inside.

twist.text: LEDs are diodes that emit light. The color depends on the semiconductor material — not a filter.

climax.text: Zener diodes break down at a precise voltage, making them perfect voltage regulators for sensitive circuits.

punchline.text: One direction only. The simplest semiconductor changed everything.

quiz.question: How do LEDs produce different colors of light?
options: Colored filters placed over white-emitting diodes change the output
Different semiconductor materials emit different wavelengths of light
Varying the current changes the color from the same material

topics.title: Circuit Breakers: Protecting Wires from Fire

hook.text: A 15-amp circuit breaker trips when current exceeds 15 amps. Without it, your walls would catch fire.

buildup.text: Excess current heats wires. If wire insulation melts before anything trips, the exposed metal sparks against wood framing.

discovery.text: Thermal breakers use a bimetallic strip that bends with heat. When current is too high, the strip trips a mechanical switch.

twist.text: Magnetic breakers react in milliseconds to short circuits. Thermal ones handle slow overloads. Modern breakers combine both.

climax.text: Arc-fault breakers detect dangerous arcing — sparks from loose connections. They prevent fires that standard breakers miss.

punchline.text: Too much current? Click. Power off. House saved.

quiz.question: What can arc-fault circuit breakers detect that standard breakers cannot?
options: Water leaks that could cause short circuits in walls
Dangerous sparking from loose connections that could start fires
Voltage spikes from lightning strikes on power lines

topics.title: How a Coal Power Plant Works

hook.text: A coal plant burns rock to boil water to spin a magnet to push electrons. Four steps to make electricity.

buildup.text: Pulverized coal burns at 1,400 degrees C. The heat boils water into high-pressure steam that drives a turbine.

discovery.text: The turbine spins a generator at 3,000 rpm. Electromagnetic induction converts mechanical energy into electrical current.

twist.text: Even the best coal plants waste 60% of fuel energy as heat. Cooling towers dump it into the atmosphere.

climax.text: Coal still generates 36% of global electricity. It's cheap but produces more CO2 per kilowatt than any other source.

punchline.text: Burn rock. Boil water. Spin magnets. That's most of the grid.

quiz.question: Why do coal power plants waste 60% of fuel energy?
options: Coal burns incompletely, leaving unburned carbon in the ash
Thermodynamic limits and cooling losses dump most heat into the atmosphere
Friction in the generator converts most energy into unwanted vibration

topics.title: Nuclear Power: Splitting Atoms for Steam

hook.text: A nuclear plant is a steam engine. The only difference is the heat source: uranium instead of coal.

buildup.text: Uranium-235 atoms split when hit by a neutron, releasing energy and more neutrons. A chain reaction sustains itself.

discovery.text: Control rods absorb neutrons to regulate the reaction. Push them in to slow down; pull them out to speed up.

twist.text: One kilogram of uranium produces as much energy as 20,000 kilograms of coal — with zero CO2 during operation.

climax.text: France generates 70% of its electricity from nuclear plants. It has some of the cheapest, cleanest power in Europe.

punchline.text: Split an atom. Boil water. Same steam turbine as coal.

quiz.question: How much coal energy does one kilogram of uranium replace?
options: About 100 kilograms of coal equivalent
About 20,000 kilograms of coal equivalent
About 1 million kilograms of coal equivalent

topics.title: Solar Panels: Photons to Electrons

hook.text: A solar panel has no moving parts. Sunlight hits silicon and electrons start flowing. Pure solid-state magic.

buildup.text: Photons knock electrons loose in the silicon. A built-in electric field at the P-N junction sweeps them into a circuit.

discovery.text: Bell Labs made the first practical solar cell in 1954. It converted 6% of sunlight to electricity.

twist.text: Modern panels exceed 22% efficiency. Perovskite cells in labs reach 33%. Costs dropped 99% since 1976.

climax.text: Solar is now the cheapest electricity source in most countries. It's cheaper than running existing coal plants.

punchline.text: Light hits silicon. Electrons flow. No combustion needed.

quiz.question: How have solar panel costs changed since 1976?
options: They dropped about 50%, making them competitive with gas
They dropped 99%, making solar the cheapest source in most countries
They stayed roughly the same but efficiency gains offset costs

topics.title: Wind Turbines: Harvesting Moving Air

hook.text: A single offshore wind turbine can power 16,000 homes. Its blades sweep an area larger than a football field.

buildup.text: Wind pushes the blades, spinning a rotor connected to a generator. Aerodynamic lift, not drag, does most of the work.

discovery.text: The Betz limit says no turbine can capture more than 59.3% of wind energy. Modern turbines reach about 45%.

twist.text: Power increases with the cube of wind speed. Double the wind speed and you get eight times the power output.

climax.text: Denmark generates over 50% of its electricity from wind. Some days it produces more wind power than it consumes.

punchline.text: Catch the wind. Spin a magnet. Free electricity forever.

quiz.question: What happens to a wind turbine's power output when wind speed doubles?
options: Power output doubles proportionally with wind speed
Power increases by eight times since it scales with the cube of wind speed
Power triples because the blades spin three times faster

topics.title: Hydroelectric Power: Gravity Does the Work

hook.text: The Three Gorges Dam in China generates 22,500 MW — enough to power the entire country of Norway.

buildup.text: Water falls from a reservoir through turbines. Gravity pulls it down; the turbine converts that motion to electricity.

discovery.text: Hydroelectric turbines are over 90% efficient — the highest of any generation technology. Very little energy is wasted.

twist.text: Dams flood valleys, displace communities, and block fish migration. The environmental cost is significant.

climax.text: Pumped storage hydro uses excess grid power to pump water uphill, then releases it during peak demand. It's a giant battery.

punchline.text: Water falls. Turbines spin. Gravity never stops working.

quiz.question: How does pumped-storage hydropower act like a giant battery?
options: It stores water in pressurized underground tanks for later release
Excess power pumps water uphill, which is released through turbines during peak demand
Chemical reactions in the reservoir store electrical energy as heat

topics.title: Batteries: Storing Electrons Chemically

hook.text: A lithium-ion battery stores energy in chemical bonds. Charging forces lithium ions one way; discharging sends them back.

buildup.text: Two electrodes — an anode and a cathode — sit in an electrolyte. Ions shuttle between them carrying charge.

discovery.text: John Goodenough invented the lithium cobalt oxide cathode in 1980. He received the Nobel Prize in 2019 — at age 97.

twist.text: Lithium-ion batteries degrade with every cycle. After 1,000 charges, capacity drops to about 80% of original.

climax.text: Solid-state batteries replace liquid electrolyte with a solid. They promise double the energy density and no fire risk.

punchline.text: Chemistry stores electricity. Ions shuttle back and forth. Rechargeable.

quiz.question: What advantage do solid-state batteries promise over lithium-ion?
options: They cost half as much to manufacture at scale
They offer double the energy density with no fire risk
They never degrade regardless of the number of charge cycles

topics.title: The Transistor: Switch That Built the Digital Age

hook.text: Your smartphone has 15 billion transistors. Each one is a tiny switch — on or off, 1 or 0.

buildup.text: A transistor uses a small signal to control a larger current. It amplifies or switches depending on the circuit.

discovery.text: Bardeen, Brattain, and Shockley invented it at Bell Labs in 1947. It replaced vacuum tubes that were hot and fragile.

twist.text: The first transistor was a crude germanium device. Today's are just 3 nanometers wide — 25 atoms across.

climax.text: Moore's Law predicted transistor counts would double every two years. It held true for over five decades.

punchline.text: On or off. Billions of times per second. That's computing.

quiz.question: What did the transistor replace in early electronic systems?
options: Mechanical relays that were too slow for telephone networks
Vacuum tubes that were hot, fragile, and power-hungry
Copper wire switches that wore out after limited cycles

topics.title: Integrated Circuits: A Factory on a Chip

hook.text: An integrated circuit packs millions of components onto a chip smaller than your fingernail.

buildup.text: Jack Kilby and Robert Noyce independently invented the IC in 1958-59. Kilby used germanium; Noyce used silicon.

discovery.text: Photolithography prints circuit patterns with UV light on silicon wafers. Each layer adds transistors, resistors, and wires.

twist.text: A modern chip factory costs $20 billion. Only three companies on Earth can build leading-edge chips.

climax.text: TSMC in Taiwan manufactures chips for Apple, AMD, and Nvidia. A single disruption could halt the global tech industry.

punchline.text: Print circuits with light. Shrink them every year. Run the world.

quiz.question: Why are modern chip factories so expensive to build?
options: They require rare raw materials imported from only one country
Photolithography at nanometer scales demands extremely precise and costly equipment
Government regulations require extensive safety certifications

topics.title: Sensors: Machines That Feel the World

hook.text: Your phone has at least 14 sensors: accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer, barometer, and more.

buildup.text: A sensor converts a physical quantity — temperature, pressure, light — into an electrical signal a circuit can read.

discovery.text: MEMS sensors are microscopic machines etched into silicon. A phone's accelerometer has a tiny mass on a spring.

twist.text: MEMS accelerometers cost under $1 each. In the 1990s, equivalent sensors cost thousands and filled a desktop.

climax.text: IoT devices embed sensors in bridges, factories, and farms. Billions of sensors now feed data to the cloud continuously.

punchline.text: Feel light, heat, motion, pressure. Convert it to numbers. That's sensing.

quiz.question: What are MEMS sensors?
options: Large industrial sensors mounted on factory equipment
Microscopic machines etched into silicon that detect physical quantities
Software algorithms that simulate sensor behavior digitally

topics.title: Op-Amps: The Swiss Army Knife of Electronics

hook.text: An operational amplifier costs 10 cents and does everything: amplify, filter, compare, and compute.

buildup.text: An op-amp has two inputs and one output. It amplifies the difference between the inputs by a huge factor.

discovery.text: Negative feedback tames the gain. By connecting output to input through a resistor, you get precise, controllable amplification.

twist.text: The original op-amp filled a room and cost $1,000 in 1941. The LM741, introduced in 1968, costs pennies.

climax.text: Audio equipment, medical instruments, and control systems all depend on op-amps. They're in virtually every analog circuit.

punchline.text: Two inputs, one output, infinite uses. The op-amp does it all.

quiz.question: How does negative feedback improve an operational amplifier?
options: It increases the op-amp's maximum output voltage range
It provides precise, controllable amplification by taming the raw gain
It reduces the power consumption of the amplifier circuit

topics.title: Power Electronics: Converting Power Efficiently

hook.text: Your laptop charger converts 240V AC from the wall into 20V DC for your battery. It loses less than 10% as heat.

buildup.text: Switching converters chop DC into high-frequency AC, transform it, and rectify it back. The trick is speed.

discovery.text: At high frequencies, transformers shrink dramatically. That's why modern chargers are tiny compared to old brick adapters.

twist.text: Gallium nitride transistors switch faster and waste less heat than silicon. GaN chargers are half the size at the same power.

climax.text: Inverters in EVs and solar systems use power electronics to convert DC to AC. Efficiency determines range and output.

punchline.text: Chop, transform, rectify. Fast switching makes power conversion tiny.

quiz.question: Why are gallium nitride chargers smaller than silicon-based ones?
options: GaN conducts electricity with zero resistance like a superconductor
GaN transistors switch faster and waste less heat, enabling smaller components
GaN is a lighter material reducing the weight and volume

topics.title: Microcontrollers: Computers the Size of a Stamp

hook.text: A microcontroller has a processor, memory, and I/O on a single chip. Your microwave has one. So does your toothbrush.

buildup.text: Unlike PCs, microcontrollers run one program forever. They boot in milliseconds and use milliwatts of power.

discovery.text: The Arduino made microcontrollers accessible. A $25 board lets anyone program hardware without an engineering degree.

twist.text: There are more microcontrollers on Earth than people. Over 30 billion are embedded in devices worldwide.

climax.text: Self-driving cars use dozens of microcontrollers for brakes, steering, sensors, and communication. Each one is safety-critical.

punchline.text: A full computer for under a dollar. In everything you own.

quiz.question: How many microcontrollers are estimated to exist worldwide?
options: About 1 billion, roughly one per eight people
Over 30 billion, far more than the global human population
About 500 million, concentrated in smartphones and laptops

topics.title: How the Power Grid Works

hook.text: The electrical grid is the largest machine ever built. It delivers power to billions of people every second.

buildup.text: Generation, transmission, and distribution form three layers. Power stations feed high-voltage lines that feed local substations.

discovery.text: Supply must exactly equal demand at every instant. If generation falls short, frequency drops and blackouts cascade.

twist.text: Grid operators balance supply and demand by dispatching power plants in real time. It's like conducting a live orchestra.

climax.text: Renewable energy makes balancing harder. Wind and solar vary constantly, requiring storage and flexible backup plants.

punchline.text: Generate it, move it, balance it. Every second of every day.

quiz.question: What happens when electricity supply falls below demand on the grid?
options: Voltage increases to compensate for the reduced current flow
Grid frequency drops and cascading blackouts can result
Electricity is automatically imported from neighboring countries

topics.title: Blackouts: When the Grid Fails

hook.text: The 2003 Northeast blackout cut power to 55 million people. The cause was a software bug and one sagging tree.

buildup.text: A power line sagged into an overgrown tree in Ohio. The alarm system had a software bug and didn't alert operators.

discovery.text: Cascading failure followed. Overloaded lines tripped, shifting load to others, which also tripped. Dominoes across eight states.

twist.text: The blackout lasted up to four days in some areas. Eleven people died. Economic losses exceeded $6 billion.

climax.text: New reliability standards now require vegetation management, better monitoring, and mandatory reporting of grid events.

punchline.text: One tree. One bug. 55 million people in the dark.

quiz.question: What triggered the 2003 Northeast blackout?
options: A cyberattack on the power grid's control systems
A power line sagging into a tree combined with a software alarm bug
A nuclear plant emergency shutdown that overloaded the grid

topics.title: Smart Grids: The Grid Gets a Brain

hook.text: The traditional grid is blind — operators don't know a line is down until someone calls to complain.

buildup.text: Smart grids add sensors and communication to every node. Meters, switches, and transformers report status in real time.

discovery.text: Smart meters track usage every 15 minutes. Utilities can adjust pricing to shift demand away from peak hours.

twist.text: Self-healing grids detect faults and reroute power automatically. Outages that lasted hours now last seconds.

climax.text: Smart grids integrate rooftop solar, EVs, and home batteries. Your house can sell power back to the grid.

punchline.text: Give the grid sensors and software. It manages itself.

quiz.question: How do self-healing smart grids improve reliability?
options: They store emergency power in underground batteries throughout the network
They detect faults and reroute power automatically, reducing outage times to seconds
They limit total power usage to prevent any section from overloading

topics.title: Energy Storage: The Grid's Missing Piece

hook.text: The grid has no warehouse. Electricity must be used the instant it's generated — unless you store it.

buildup.text: Lithium-ion batteries dominate grid storage now. Tesla's Hornsdale battery in Australia stabilizes the grid and earns profit.

discovery.text: Flow batteries use liquid electrolytes in tanks. Scale them up just by adding more liquid — independent of power rating.

twist.text: Gravity storage lifts heavy blocks with excess energy and drops them to generate power later. Astonishingly simple.

climax.text: Affordable storage is the key to 100% renewable grids. Without it, solar and wind can't replace fossil fuels.

punchline.text: Generate when the wind blows. Use it when the wind stops. Storage bridges the gap.

quiz.question: How does gravity-based energy storage work?
options: Compressed air is pumped underground and released through turbines
Heavy blocks are lifted with excess energy and dropped to generate power later
Water is frozen at night and melted during the day to spin generators

topics.title: Microgrids: Going Off the Main Grid

hook.text: A microgrid powers a campus, hospital, or village independently. If the main grid fails, the microgrid keeps running.

buildup.text: Microgrids combine solar panels, batteries, and backup generators into a self-contained power system.

discovery.text: An island switch disconnects the microgrid from the main grid during outages. It operates autonomously until power returns.

twist.text: When Hurricane Maria wrecked Puerto Rico's grid, it stayed down for months. Microgrids at hospitals kept critical services alive.

climax.text: Military bases, remote communities, and data centers use microgrids for energy security. Independence from the grid is strategic.

punchline.text: Your own little grid. Works when the big one doesn't.

quiz.question: What proved the value of microgrids during Hurricane Maria?
options: Microgrids transmitted power from the mainland to the island
Hospitals and shelters with microgrids maintained power when the main grid collapsed
Microgrid batteries charged cell phones for millions of residents

topics.title: Wireless Power: Cutting the Last Cord

hook.text: Nikola Tesla dreamed of sending electricity through the air. In 1901, he built Wardenclyffe Tower to try it.

buildup.text: Tesla's tower failed, but the idea survived. Inductive charging uses magnetic fields to transfer energy wirelessly.

discovery.text: MIT researchers sent 60 watts across a room in 2007. They lit a light bulb with no wires at all.

twist.text: Wireless phone chargers already use this. But efficiency drops fast with distance — most energy becomes heat.

climax.text: Some roads now charge electric buses as they drive. Coils buried under the road transfer power to the vehicle.

punchline.text: Tesla's dream wasn't wrong. It was just early.

quiz.question: What was significant about MIT's 2007 wireless power experiment?
options: They wirelessly charged a car battery from 50 meters away
They transferred 60 watts across a room to light a bulb with no wires
They proved Tesla's tower design would have worked
